The alumnus answered with a single line and offered an introduction to a colleague. I can't say what Abhinav was hoping for, but the room was quieter and the notebook fuller than usual.

passage:
Week one. Nirmala, a lab technician wanting to move into clinical research, found an alumnus from her college on a professional networking site: Pankaj, a clinical research associate at a hospital in Hyderabad. She wrote three lines: who she was, what she hoped to learn, and "Could I have fifteen minutes on a call, any day that suits you?"
Week two. Pankaj agreed to a Saturday morning call. She had written five questions. He told her things no job ad had: that most entry roles start in site coordination, that one short certificate mattered more than a second degree, and that people in the field notice anyone who documents carefully.
The same evening Nirmala emailed him a short summary: "What I learned: 1. Start in site coordination. 2. Get the certificate. 3. Keep clean records. Thank you."
Week five. Pankaj forwarded her a site coordinator opening with a note: "You seemed serious. Apply."

qa.q: What did Pankaj say mattered more than a second degree?
qa.a: He said one short certificate mattered more than a second degree.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt when writing to someone she'd never met?
qa.a: She may have felt nervous and hopeful, keeping the message short and polite and asking only for fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What else could Nirmala do to keep the connection helpful?
qa.a: She could send Pankaj a brief update when she finishes the certificate, keeping the relationship alive without asking for too much.

qa.q: How did Nirmala's summary email look to Pankaj?
qa.a: Pankaj saw someone who listened carefully and followed up, which is why he felt she was serious enough to forward an opening.

grounding: Shows the person writing to an alumnus in the target field, having a short call and following up with a summary of what was learned.

subtype: Approach: find a mentor in the target field [Action]
passage:
"Chetan, you're wondering how I got into policy research from engineering? Sit, have some chai. I'm Rehana, and I was twenty-two and completely lost.
I had no one in that world. So I found our college alumni list and saw one name, a woman who'd done the same switch ten years before. I wrote to her. Short. Who I was, why I admired her path, and could she spare fifteen minutes. I nearly didn't send it.
She said yes. On that call she told me things I'd never have found online: that writing samples mattered more than grades, that the good jobs were rarely posted, and that I should volunteer at one think tank's events.
That night I emailed her a summary of what I learned and thanked her. She remembered that. Six months later she recommended me for an internship.
So, write to someone. Keep it short. And always send the summary."

qa.q: What did the alumna say mattered more than grades?
qa.a: She said writing samples mattered more than grades.

qa.q: How did young Rehana feel before sending the message?
qa.a: Rehana felt lost and nervous, nearly not sending the message at all.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Rehana's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Sending the summary email after the call was the turning point, because the alumna remembered it and later recommended Rehana for an internship.

qa.q: How might the alumna have felt receiving Rehana's summary email?
qa.a: She likely felt appreciated and impressed that her advice was taken seriously, which made her willing to help again.

grounding: Shows a person writing to an alumnus in the desired field, taking a short call and following up with a summary, which reveals unwritten rules.
